assessment.nobel_worthiness: Collateral constraints that amplify and propagate shocks (Kiyotaki-Moore) and the financial-accelerator and intermediary-frictions tradition (Gertler and co-authors) became the standard way macroeconomics models credit and financial frictions. The work changed how business cycles, crises and policy are analysed and has been tested against the 2008 crisis and its aftermath. Its influence on both theory and applied policy modelling is very broad.
assessment.attribution: The credit-cycle mechanism is most clearly credited to Kiyotaki and Moore. Gertler's contribution runs through the accelerator and later intermediary models, and the Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist lineage overlaps with prior recognition of Bernanke. Gilchrist is excluded because the three-person limit and the weight of the core mechanism favour the other three. This is a defensible but not unique split.
assessment.maturity: The core papers date from the 1990s, so the ideas have had ample time to prove durable and to be extended empirically. The post-2008 vindication adds to this. Timing is not a concern.
uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers to credit Gertler or the Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist accelerator line, given Bernanke's earlier prize.
Overlap with the New Keynesian ballot on Gertler's credit.
I have not independently verified the citation or influence figures; this rests on general knowledge.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The random-coefficients demand framework (BLP) and the dynamic industry models of Pakes and co-authors turned industrial organisation into a quantitative, structural discipline. They are used for merger review, antitrust and welfare analysis, and they spread into trade, health and other fields. The methodological and practical impact is large and durable.
assessment.attribution: BLP is a clean, well-defined three-author contribution (Berry, Levinsohn, Pakes), and Pakes also has independent dynamic-model work. Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin made important but more distinct or later contributions. The core credit is relatively clear.
assessment.maturity: BLP dates from 1995 and has been used for three decades, so confirmation is extensive and the timing is ripe.
uncertainties: Whether Bresnahan's and Reiss's empirical-IO contributions deserve recognition alongside the BLP group.
Structural IO's reliance on functional-form and equilibrium assumptions may temper some enthusiasm.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The task-based view of technology and the empirical evidence on trade shocks reshaped how economists understand labour demand, wage inequality and the local costs of globalisation. The work bears directly on central policy debates and combines conceptual framing with credible empirical design. It also connects to the technology-and-inequality literature in macro.
assessment.attribution: The credit is spread across several authors and partly overlaps with the Goldin-Katz skill-premium work and with the Acemoglu task-based framework, which has been recognised in other contexts. The China-shock papers are Autor-Dorn-Hanson, while task-based labour-demand work involves Autor, Katz and others. Excluding Dorn is a close call.
assessment.maturity: The China-shock and task papers are 10-20 years old and well scrutinised. The empirical findings have been debated, refined and largely reaffirmed in broad terms, though magnitudes remain contested.
uncertainties: Overlap with prior recognition of related work, which complicates attribution.
Ongoing debate over the size and persistence of the trade-shock effects.
Whether Dorn rather than Katz should be included.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection into exporting reorganised international trade theory and its quantification. The framework introduced new gains-from-trade channels and underpins much modern empirical trade work. The influence on both theory and data analysis is very large.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the central contribution, and Helpman has a long record of foundational work in trade theory and in the firm-level extensions. Redding is important but later. Krugman's earlier prize covers the preceding new trade theory, which makes the incremental contribution distinct but related. The two-person credit seems reasonable.
assessment.maturity: More than twenty years have passed since the core papers, and the empirical firm-level evidence is extensive. Timing is fine.
uncertainties: Possible overlap with the Eaton-Kortum quantitative tradition and the Bernard-Jensen empirical origins.
Helpman also appears on the trade-politics ballot, which may dilute or concentrate support.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The nominal-rigidity framework and the New Keynesian theory of monetary policy are now central to how central banks reason and build models. Staggered pricing and wage-setting, rules-based policy and the microfounded policy framework have shaped both academic macroeconomics and practice. The influence on policy institutions is exceptional.
assessment.attribution: This is the most crowded credit structure on the list. Calvo (pricing), Taylor (staggered contracts and the policy rule), Woodford (synthesis and normative analysis), Gali, Christiano-Eichenbaum and Smets all made major contributions, and Evans, an important co-author of Christiano-Eichenbaum, is not credited here. Any three-person selection leaves out significant contributors, which is a real weakness.
assessment.maturity: The core contributions are 25-45 years old and thoroughly tested. The framework was stressed by post-2008 and post-2020 events but has been adapted rather than discarded.
uncertainties: Large attribution ambiguity and the risk of omitting central contributors.
Debate over whether the framework's forecasting and inflation-modelling record weakens the case.
Prior recognition of related monetary and expectations work.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Misallocation as an explanation of cross-country income and productivity differences provided a measurable, disciplined link between micro-level distortions and aggregate outcomes. The work transformed the development-accounting and growth agenda and spawned a large empirical and quantitative literature. It speaks to one of the central questions in economics.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh-Klenow (2009) is the best-known single contribution, with Restuccia and Rogerson (2008) a parallel and closely related paper. Rogerson is not credited on this ballot, which is a gap in the attribution. The three-person set is plausible but incomplete.
assessment.maturity: The papers are about 15-18 years old and heavily cited, but measurement of misallocation has faced critiques about measurement error and model dependence. The field is still debating magnitudes.
uncertainties: Measurement-error and model-dependence critiques of the misallocation estimates.
The omission of Rogerson from the credited names.
My own field proximity (macro and growth) could bias my assessment toward the topic; I have tried to apply common criteria.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: A systematic, theory-and-evidence programme on how electoral rules, constitutions and state capacity shape fiscal policy and economic outcomes. It established modern political economics as a mainstream field and links institutions to policy and development. The breadth and rigour are substantial.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini are the central pair through their joint books and papers, and Besley's contributions (including with Persson on state capacity) are closely linked. The attribution is reasonably clean, though Besley's own work is partly distinct.
assessment.maturity: The work dates from the 1990s-2010s and is well established. Recent prizes in institutions and growth show the committee's interest, but this also raises the question of how much adjacent recognition is appropriate.
uncertainties: Possible proximity of the topic to recently recognised institutions-and-growth work.
Potential personal and institutional connections between committee members and the candidates, which I note but do not adjudicate; the profile does not document any specific relationship for me.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population-scale administrative data used to measure intergenerational mobility and neighbourhood effects changed what can be established about opportunity and inequality. The work is empirically influential, policy-relevant and methodologically innovative in its use of data. The topic is central to the study of inequality.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the clear leading contributor, with Hendren and Friedman as long-standing co-authors on the main mobility and neighbourhood papers. Katz, credited here, has a separate and perhaps stronger case on another ballot. The credit is concentrated on Chetty, but separating co-author contributions is hard.
assessment.maturity: The central papers are from roughly 2014-2022, so the evidence is comparatively young. Replication and long-run follow-up of the neighbourhood effects are still developing, and some critiques of the mobility measures remain.
uncertainties: Relative recency compared with other ballots.
Debate over measurement choices and causal interpretation of neighbourhood effects.
How the committee would split credit among Chetty and his many co-authors.
